chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — A hall in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Enter Duke, Egeon, Jailer, Officers and other Attendants.]
EGEON. Go ahead, Solinus, sentence me to die, and let the verdict of death end my sorrows along with my life.

DUKE. Merchant of Syracuse, stop pleading. I won't bend our laws. The hostility and conflict that recently sprang from your Duke's vicious crackdown on merchants — our honest countrymen, who lacked the gold to ransom themselves and so sealed his harsh decrees with their blood — has shut out all pity from our stern looks. Ever since the deadly, civil-style feud between your seditious countrymen and us began, it has been formally decreed, by both the Syracusans and ourselves, that no trade is permitted between our enemy towns. Furthermore: if any native of Ephesus is seen at Syracusan markets and fairs, or if any native Syracusan comes to the bay of Ephesus, he dies. His goods are seized by the Duke, unless a thousand marks are paid to lift the penalty and ransom him. Your possessions, valued at the highest rate, can't amount to a hundred marks. Therefore, by law you are condemned to die.
EGEON. Yet here's my comfort: when your words are done, my sorrows will end with the setting sun.
DUKE. Well, Syracusan, tell me briefly why you left your homeland, and why you came to Ephesus.

EGEON. A heavier task could not have been imposed on me than to speak my unspeakable griefs. Still, so the world may witness that my end was caused by fate, not by any vile crime, I'll tell what my sorrow allows me to say. I was born in Syracuse, and married to a woman who would have been happy — except for me, and through no fault but our bad luck. I lived with her in joy. Our wealth grew through the successful voyages I often made to Epidamnum, until my agent there died and the great burden of unmanaged goods drew me away from my wife's embrace. I had not been gone six months before she — almost ready to faint under the pleasant burden women bear — made arrangements to follow me, and soon arrived safely where I was. She had not been there long before she became the joyful mother of two fine sons, and — strangely — one looked so like the other that they could be told apart only by their names. In that very same hour, and at the same inn, a poor woman gave birth to a similar pair, male twins, also identical. Because their parents were extremely poor, I bought them and raised them to wait on my sons. My wife, not a little proud of two such boys, asked daily that we go home. Reluctantly, I agreed; alas, too soon. We had sailed only a league from Epidamnum before the always-obedient sea gave any tragic sign of our coming disaster. But we soon lost much hope, for what little light the heavens granted only brought to our terrified minds a near-certain warning of immediate death — which I myself would gladly have embraced, but the constant weeping of my wife, weeping in anticipation of what she saw coming, and the pitiful crying of the pretty babies, who cried because that's what they saw us doing without knowing what to fear, forced me to find delays for them and for myself. And it came to this — for there was no other option. The sailors took the lifeboat to save themselves, leaving us the ship, which was on the verge of sinking. My wife, more concerned for the younger-born, had tied him to a small spare mast, the kind sailors keep on board for storms. One of the other twins was bound to him, while I had done the same with the other pair. With the children thus secured, my wife and I, keeping our eyes fixed on the children we cared for, tied ourselves to either end of the mast, and floating along, carried by the current, were swept towards Corinth, as we thought. At last the sun, gazing on the earth, dispersed those threatening clouds, and by the help of its welcome light the seas grew calm. We spotted two ships in the distance, racing toward us — one from Corinth, the other from Epidaurus. But before they reached us — oh, let me say no more! Guess the rest from what came before.
DUKE. No, go on, old man, don't break off like that. We may pity, even if we cannot pardon you.

EGEON. Oh, had the gods done so, I would not now rightly call them merciless to us. For before the ships could close to within ten leagues, we crashed into a mighty rock, and as we were violently thrown against it our rescue-ship was split down the middle. So that, in this cruel separation, Fortune had left each of us an equal share of joy and grief. My wife's portion — poor soul — appeared burdened with less weight, but not less sorrow. She was carried more swiftly before the wind, and we saw the three of them picked up by fishermen of Corinth, as we believed. At length another ship caught up with us; and knowing whose lives they had the luck to save, they gave us a warm welcome aboard, and would have taken the prize from the fishermen, had their boat not been very slow under sail. So instead they turned and headed home. Thus you have heard how I was cut off from my happiness, my life prolonged by misfortune only to tell sad stories of my own disasters.
DUKE. And for the sake of those you grieve for, do me the favour of telling me in full what has happened to them and to you since.

EGEON. My youngest boy, and yet my eldest worry, at eighteen began asking after his brother, and pressed me that his servant — who was in the same situation, having lost his brother but kept his name — might go with him on the search. While I, out of love, set him on his way to find the one I longed to see, I risked losing the one I already loved. Five summers I have spent in farthest Greece, roaming through the lands of Asia, and as I sailed home I came to Ephesus — hopeless of finding him, but unwilling to leave any place where men live unsearched. But here the story of my life must end. And I'd be glad to die today, if all my travels could assure me they are still alive.

DUKE. Unfortunate Egeon, whom the fates have marked for the worst of suffering. Believe me, were it not against our laws, against my crown, my oath, my dignity — which princes, even if they wished, cannot revoke — my soul would plead in your defence. But although you are sentenced to death, and that sentence cannot be reversed without great damage to our honour, I will still help you as much as I can. Therefore, merchant, I'll give you this one day to seek aid. Try every friend you have in Ephesus. Beg, or borrow, to raise the sum and live; if not, then you are doomed to die. Jailer, take him into custody.
JAILER. I will, my lord.
EGEON. Hopeless and helpless Egeon goes, only to delay his lifeless end.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — A public place
paragraphs: [Enter Antipholus and Dromio of Syracuse and a Merchant.]

MERCHANT. So put it about that you're from Epidamnum, or your goods will be seized too soon. This very day a Syracusan merchant has been arrested for arriving here, and because he can't buy back his life, the town's law says he dies before the weary sun sets in the west. Here's the money you left me to look after.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Take it to the Centaur, where we're lodged, and wait there, Dromio, until I come to you. It'll be dinnertime within the hour. Until then, I'll observe the customs of the town, look over the traders, gaze at the buildings, then return and sleep at my inn — long travel has left me stiff and tired. Off with you.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Many a man would take you at your word and actually leave, with such a good opportunity.
[Exit Dromio.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. A trustworthy rogue, sir, who very often, when I'm dulled by worry and melancholy, lifts my mood with his cheerful jokes. Will you walk with me through the town, then come to my inn for dinner?

MERCHANT. I've been invited, sir, by certain merchants from whom I hope to do good business. Forgive me. Later, at five o'clock, if it suits you, I'll meet you at the market, and keep your company till bedtime. My present business pulls me away from you now.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Farewell till then. I'll go lose myself, and wander up and down sightseeing.
MERCHANT. Sir, I leave you to your own contentment.
[Exit Merchant.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. He who leaves me to my own contentment leaves me to the very thing I cannot find. In this world, I'm like a drop of water in the ocean searching for another drop, who, failing to find his fellow, unseen and questing, loses himself. So I, searching for a mother and a brother, in my search for them, unhappily, lose myself.
[Enter Dromio of Ephesus.]
Here comes the almanac that tells my exact age. What now? How is it you're back so soon?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Back so soon? More like arrived too late. The chicken's burning, the pig's falling off the spit, the clock has struck twelve, and my mistress has struck one on my cheek. She's so hot because the meat's cold; the meat's cold because you're not home; you're not home because you have no appetite; you have no appetite because you've already eaten — but those of us who know what it is to fast and pray are doing penance for your no-show today.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Catch your breath, sir, and tell me this, please: where did you leave the money I gave you?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Oh, the sixpence I had last Wednesday to pay the saddler for my mistress's crupper? The saddler got it, sir, I didn't keep it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I'm not in a joking mood right now. Tell me, and don't play around — where is the money? We're strangers here. How dare you let so great a sum out of your own keeping?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Please save the jokes for when you're sitting at dinner, sir. I've come to you in a rush from my mistress. If I go back empty-handed, I'll be a post indeed, for she'll chalk up your fault on my skull. It seems to me your stomach, like mine, should be your clock, and strike you homeward without need of a messenger.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Come on, Dromio, these jokes are out of place. Save them for a happier hour than this. Where is the gold I put in your charge?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. To me, sir? Why, you gave no gold to me!
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Come on, you knave, stop the foolishness and tell me what you've done with what I gave you.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. My only job was to fetch you from the market home to your house, the Phoenix, sir, for dinner. My mistress and her sister are waiting for you.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Now, as I'm a Christian, answer me: in what safe place have you stowed my money, or I'll break that grinning head of yours that plays tricks when I'm in no mood for them. Where are the thousand marks you had from me?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I have some marks of yours on my skull, and some of my mistress's marks on my shoulders, but not a thousand marks between the two of you. If I had to pay your worship those back, you wouldn't take them patiently.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Your mistress's marks? What mistress do you have, slave?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Your worship's wife, my mistress at the Phoenix. She who fasts till you come home to dinner, and prays that you'll hurry home for dinner.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What, you'll mock me to my face after I've told you not to? There — take that, you knave.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. What do you mean, sir? For God's sake, hold your hands! No, since you won't, sir, I'll take to my heels.
[Exit Dromio.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. By my life, by some scheme or other the villain has been swindled out of all my money. They say this town is full of cheats — quick jugglers who deceive the eye, dark-working sorcerers who twist the mind, soul-killing witches who deform the body, disguised swindlers, babbling con-men, and many other such permissive sins. If it proves so, I'll leave the sooner. I'll go to the Centaur to look for this slave. I greatly fear my money is not safe.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — A public place
paragraphs: [Enter Adriana, wife to Antipholus of Ephesus, with Luciana her sister.]
ADRIANA. Neither my husband, nor the slave I sent in such haste to find his master, has come back? It must be two o'clock by now, Luciana.

LUCIANA. Perhaps some merchant has invited him, and he's gone somewhere for dinner straight from the market. Good sister, let's eat and not worry. A man is master of his own freedom; time is their master, and when they see the time, they'll come and go. If that's how it is, be patient, sister.
ADRIANA. Why should their freedom be greater than ours?
LUCIANA. Because their business is always outdoors.
ADRIANA. See, when I treat him that way, he takes it badly.
LUCIANA. Oh, understand — he's the bridle on your will.
ADRIANA. Only donkeys allow themselves to be bridled like that.

LUCIANA. Why, headstrong freedom gets whipped with sorrow. There is nothing under heaven's eye that doesn't have its limit — on earth, in the sea, in the sky. The beasts, the fishes, and the winged birds are subject to their males and at their command. Men, more godlike, are masters of all these, lords of the wide world and the wild watery seas, gifted with intellect and souls more excellent than fish and birds. They are masters and lords over their women. So let your will fall in line with theirs.
ADRIANA. This is the slavery that keeps you unmarried.
LUCIANA. Not this — the troubles of the marriage bed.
ADRIANA. But if you were married, you'd want some control.
LUCIANA. Before I learn love, I'll practise obedience.
ADRIANA. What if your husband strayed elsewhere?
LUCIANA. Until he came home again, I'd wait.

ADRIANA. Patience without a scratch! No wonder she pauses; it's easy to be meek when you've nothing to push back against. A wretched soul bruised by bad luck — we tell them to be quiet when we hear them cry. But if we carried the same weight of pain, we'd complain as much or more. So you, who have no unkind mate to grieve you, would relieve me by urging useless patience. But if you live to see your own rights stripped away, this fool's patience will be the first thing you drop.
LUCIANA. Well, I'll marry one day, just to try it. Here's your man — your husband must be near.
[Enter Dromio of Ephesus.]
ADRIANA. Tell me, is your tardy master at hand?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. No, he's at fists with me — and my two ears can vouch for it.
ADRIANA. Tell me, did you speak with him? Do you know his mind?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Yes, yes, he told me his mind right on my ear. Damn his hand, I could barely understand it.
LUCIANA. Did he speak so unclearly you couldn't feel his meaning?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. No, he struck so plainly I felt his blows all too well — and yet so unclearly that I could hardly understand them.
ADRIANA. But tell me, please, is he coming home? It seems he takes great care to please his wife.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Why, mistress, my master is surely horn-mad.
ADRIANA. Horn-mad, you villain?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I don't mean cuckold-mad, but he's stark raving mad. When I asked him to come home to dinner, he demanded a thousand marks in gold. "It's dinner time," said I. "My gold," said he. "Your meat is burning," said I. "My gold," said he. "Will you come home?" said I. "My gold," said he. "Where are the thousand marks I gave you, villain?" "The pig," said I, "is burned." "My gold," said he. "My mistress, sir," said I. "Hang your mistress! I don't know your mistress! Out on your mistress!"
LUCIANA. Said who?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Said my master. "I know," said he, "no house, no wife, no mistress." So the message that should have gone home on my tongue, I carried home — thanks to him — on my shoulders. Because, in the end, he beat me there.
ADRIANA. Go back again, slave, and fetch him home.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Go back again, and be beaten home all over again? For God's sake, send another messenger.
ADRIANA. Get back, slave, or I'll crack open your skull.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. And he'll bless that crack with another beating. Between the two of you, I'll have a holy head.
ADRIANA. Off with you, you babbling peasant. Fetch your master home.

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Am I so round with you as you are with me, that you kick me about like a football? You kick me away from here, and he'll kick me back. If I last in this job, you'll have to case me in leather.
[Exit.]
LUCIANA. Shame — see how impatience darkens your face.

ADRIANA. His company must be making his mistresses happy, while I starve at home for one cheerful look from him. Has homely old age stolen the alluring beauty from my poor cheeks? Then he's worn it out. Is my conversation dull? My wit barren? If lively, sharp talk is ruined in me, his unkindness has blunted it harder than marble. Do their fancy clothes bait his affections? That's not my fault — he controls my wardrobe. What is ruined in me that wasn't ruined by him? Then he is the cause of my decay. One sunny look from him would soon repair my withered beauty. But the unruly deer breaks the fence and feeds away from home; poor me, I'm only his stale leftover.
LUCIANA. Self-harming jealousy! Shame — drive it out.

ADRIANA. Only the unfeeling can shrug off wrongs like these. I know his eye is paying respects elsewhere — what else could be keeping him away from here? Sister, you know he promised me a chain. I'd give up that gift, even a portion of his love, if only he'd keep faith with our bed. I see that even the most beautifully enamelled jewel loses its beauty in time; yet the gold underneath endures even what others touch — though frequent touching will wear gold thin. And no man with a good name shames it through dishonesty and corruption — and yet so it goes. Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep what's left of it away, and weeping, die.
LUCIANA. How many doting fools jealousy drives to madness!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Antipholus of Syracuse.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. The gold I gave to Dromio is safely stowed at the Centaur, and the careful slave has gone out anxious to find me. By the clock and the innkeeper's account, I haven't been able to speak with Dromio since I first sent him from the market. Look, here he comes.
[Enter Dromio of Syracuse.]

How now, sir! Has your joking mood changed? If you love a beating, joke with me again. You know no Centaur? You received no gold? Your mistress sent for me to come home to dinner? My house is the Phoenix? Were you mad, that you answered me so madly?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. What answer, sir? When did I say any such thing?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Just now, right here, less than half an hour ago.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I haven't seen you since you sent me off home to the Centaur with the gold you gave me.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Villain, you denied receiving the gold, and told me about a mistress and a dinner — for which I hope you felt how displeased I was.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I'm glad to see you in such a cheerful mood. What's this joke about? Please, master, tell me.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. So, you mock and jeer at me to my face? You think I'm joking? Here, take that — and that.
[Beats Dromio.]
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Stop, sir, for God's sake! Now your joke is serious. What's this beating for?

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Because sometimes I treat you familiarly, like my fool, and chat with you, your cheekiness takes liberty with my goodwill and turns my serious hours into a free-for-all. When the sun shines, let foolish gnats sport about; but creep into crannies when he hides his beams. If you want to joke with me, read my mood, and shape your behaviour to my expression — or I'll beat that lesson into your skull.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Skull, you call it? If you'd stop the battering, I'd rather it stayed a head. If you keep up these blows, I'll have to get a fortress for my head, and fortify it too, or else I'll have to look for my brains in my shoulders. But please, sir, why am I being beaten?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Don't you know?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Nothing, sir, except that I am being beaten.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Shall I tell you why?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Yes, sir, and wherefore — they say every why has a wherefore.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why? First, for mocking me. Wherefore? For doing it a second time.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Was there ever a man so badly timed in his beating, when in the why and the wherefore there's neither rhyme nor reason? Well, sir, I thank you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Thank me, sir? For what?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, for this something you gave me for nothing.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I'll make it up to you next time by giving you nothing for something. But tell me, sir, is it dinnertime?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, sir. I think the meat is missing what I've got.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. By all means, sir — what's that?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Basting.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Well, sir, then it'll be dry.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. If it is, sir, please don't eat any of it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Your reason?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. So it doesn't make you choleric, and earn me another dry basting.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Well, sir, learn to joke at the right time. There's a time for everything.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I'd have denied that before you grew so choleric.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. By what rule, sir?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, by a rule as plain as Father Time's plain bald head itself.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Let's hear it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. There's no time for a man to recover the hair he loses by nature.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Can't he do it by fine and recovery?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Yes — pay a fine for a wig, and recover the lost hair of another man.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why is Time so stingy with hair, given how plentiful a growth it is?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Because it's a blessing he bestows on beasts, and what he's skimped on men in hair he's given them in wit.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why, but there's many a man with more hair than wit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Not one of them lacks the wit to lose his hair.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why, then you've decided that hairy men are honest dealers without wit.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. The more honest the dealer, the sooner he loses it — though he loses it in a kind of jollity.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. For what reason?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. For two — and sound ones too.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. No, not sound, please.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Sure ones, then.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. No, not sure — in a thing that lies.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Certain ones, then.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Name them.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. One, to save the money he'd spend dressing it. The other, so at dinner the hair won't drop into his porridge.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. All this time you were supposed to be proving there's no time for everything.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, and I did, sir — namely, no time at all to recover hair lost by nature.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. But your reasoning wasn't solid as to why there's no time to recover it.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Then I'll patch it up: Time himself is bald, and therefore, until the world ends, he'll have bald followers.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I knew it would be a bald conclusion. But quiet! Who's signalling us over there?
[Enter Adriana and Luciana.]

ADRIANA. Yes, yes, Antipholus, act like a stranger and frown. Some other mistress has your sweet looks. I'm not Adriana, and not your wife. There was a time when, unprompted, you would swear that no words were music to your ear, no sight pleasing to your eye, no touch welcome to your hand, no meat sweet to your taste, unless I spoke, or looked, or touched, or carved for you. How is it now, my husband, oh, how is it that you've become a stranger to yourself? Yourself, I call it — being a stranger to me, who, undivided and inseparable, am better than the better part of your dear self. Ah, don't tear yourself away from me. For know, my love, as easily can you let a drop of water fall into the gulf and take that same drop out again unchanged, neither added to nor diminished — as take yourself from me and not take me too. How deeply it would wound you, should you only hear that I were promiscuous? That this body, dedicated to you, were contaminated by rough lust? Wouldn't you spit at me, kick me, throw the name of husband in my face, tear the stained skin off my whore's forehead, cut the wedding ring from my faithless hand, and break it with a vow of divorce? I know you would; so go ahead, see that you do it. I am stained with an adulterous blot; my blood is mixed with the crime of lust. For if we two are one, and you play false, I'm digesting the poison of your flesh, made a whore by your infection. So keep faithful peace with your true bed, and I live unstained, you with your honour intact.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Are you speaking to me, fair lady? I don't know you. In Ephesus I'm only two hours old, as much a stranger to your town as to your speech. After scanning every word with all my wit, I haven't got the wit to understand a single one.
LUCIANA. Shame, brother, how the world has changed with you! Since when do you treat my sister like this? She sent for you by Dromio to come home for dinner.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. By Dromio?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By me?
ADRIANA. By you. And you brought back this reply from him: that he beat you, and in his blows denied that my house was his, and that I was his wife.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Did you talk, sir, with this gentlewoman? What's the agreement between you?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I, sir? I never saw her in my life until now.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Villain, you lie. You delivered her very words to me at the market.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I never spoke with her in my life.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Then how can she call us by our names? Unless it's by some inspired knowledge.

ADRIANA. How poorly it suits your seriousness to play along so crudely with your slave, encouraging him to thwart me in my mood. Whatever wrong I've done you, you don't have to add to that wrong with more contempt. Come, I'll cling to this sleeve of yours. You are an elm, my husband; I, a vine, whose weakness, married to your stronger frame, shares in your strength. If anything pulls you away from me, it's rubbish — usurping ivy, briar, or idle moss — which, for lack of pruning, all push in to infect your sap, and live off your decline.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. She's speaking to me; she's making me her subject. What, did I marry her in a dream? Or am I sleeping now and only think I hear this? What error has my eyes and ears so wrong? Until I'm sure about this strange uncertainty, I'll play along with the fantasy being offered.
LUCIANA. Dromio, go tell the servants to set out dinner.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Oh, where are my prayer beads! I make the sign of the cross — I'm a sinner. This is fairyland. Oh, what spite of spites! We're talking with goblins, owls, and sprites. If we don't obey, this will follow: they'll suck out our breath, or pinch us black and blue.
LUCIANA. Why are you muttering to yourself instead of answering? Dromio, you drone, you snail, you slug, you sot.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I'm transformed, master, am I not?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I think you are — in mind. So am I.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, master, in mind AND in my shape.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. You still have your own shape.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, I'm an ape.
LUCIANA. If you're changed into anything, it's an ass.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. That's true: she rides me, and I long for grass. So it is — I'm an ass, otherwise it could never be that I wouldn't know her as well as she knows me.

ADRIANA. Come, come, I won't be a fool any longer, sticking my finger in my eye and weeping while husband and slave laugh my sorrows to scorn. Come, sir, to dinner. Dromio, watch the gate. Husband, I'll dine upstairs with you today, and have you confess to a thousand idle tricks. Sirrah, if anyone asks for your master, say he's dining out, and let no living creature enter. Come, sister. Dromio, play the porter well.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Am I on earth, in heaven, or in hell? Sleeping or waking, mad, or in my right mind? Known to these people, and a stranger to myself! I'll say what they say, and play along, and through this fog I'll go wherever it leads.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, shall I be porter at the gate?
ADRIANA. Yes. And let no one in, or I'll crack your skull.
LUCIANA. Come, come, Antipholus, we're dining too late.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Antipholus of Ephesus, his man Dromio of Ephesus, Angelo the goldsmith, and Balthasar the merchant.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Good Signior Angelo, you must excuse us all. My wife is shrewish when I don't keep regular hours. Tell her I lingered at your shop watching her necklace being made, and that you'll bring it to the house tomorrow. But here's a villain who would lie to my face. He tells me he met me at the market, that I beat him, that I demanded a thousand marks in gold, and that I denied having a wife and a house. You drunkard — what did you mean by all that?

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Say what you will, sir, but I know what I know. That you beat me at the market, I have your handwriting to prove it. If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink, your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I think you're an ass.

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. By God, so it appears, from the wrongs I suffer and the blows I bear. I ought to kick when I'm kicked; and since that's how things stand, you'd best keep clear of my heels and beware of an ass.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You're glum, Signior Balthasar. Pray God our food matches my goodwill and your warm welcome here.
BALTHASAR. I rate your fine food cheap, sir, and your welcome dear.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Oh, Signior Balthasar, with meat or fish, a tableful of welcome hardly makes one fine dish.
BALTHASAR. Good meat, sir, is common; every peasant provides it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. And welcome is even more common, since that's nothing but words.
BALTHASAR. A modest meal and a great welcome make for a merry feast.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Yes — with a stingy host and a guest who eats little. But though my dishes are humble, take them in good spirit. You may get a better meal elsewhere, but not with better-hearted hosting. But wait — my door is locked. Go tell them to let us in.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Maud, Bridget, Marian, Cicely, Gillian, Ginn!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE.
[Within.] Dolt, work-horse, capon, coxcomb, idiot, fool!
Either get away from the door, or sit down at the hatch. Are you conjuring up wenches, calling for so many when one is one too many? Go, get away from the door.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. What fool has been made our porter? My master is waiting in the street.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Let him walk back where he came from, before he catches cold in his feet.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Who's talking in there? Hey, open the door!
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Right, sir, I'll tell you when — if you'll tell me why.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Why? For my dinner. I haven't eaten today.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Nor will you eat here today; come back when you can.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. What are you that keeps me out of the house I own?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. The porter for the moment, sir, and my name is Dromio.

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Oh, villain! You've stolen both my job and my name. The first never earned me credit, the second plenty of blame. If you'd been Dromio in my place today, you'd have traded your face for a name, or your name for an ass's.
[Enter Luce, concealed from Antipholus of Ephesus and his companions.]
LUCE.
[Within.] What a racket there, Dromio. Who are those at the gate?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Let my master in, Luce.
LUCE. Honestly, no — he comes too late. Tell your master so.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Oh Lord, I have to laugh. Here's a proverb for you: shall I set in my staff?
LUCE. Here's another for you: when? — can you tell?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. If your name is Luce — Luce, you've answered him well.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Do you hear, you minx? You will let us in, I hope?
LUCE. I thought I was the one to be asked.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. And you said no.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. So — come, lend a hand. Well struck — blow for blow.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You baggage, let me in.
LUCE. Can you tell me for whose sake?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Master, knock the door hard.
LUCE. Let him knock till it aches.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You'll cry for this, minx, if I beat down the door.
LUCE. What's the need of all that, when the town has stocks for offenders?
[Enter Adriana, concealed from Antipholus of Ephesus and his companions.]
ADRIANA.
[Within.] Who's at the door making all this noise?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Honestly, your town is plagued with unruly boys.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Are you there, wife? You might have come sooner.
ADRIANA. Your wife, you knave? Go, get away from the door.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. If you were in pain, master, this knave would be sore indeed.
ANGELO. Here's neither food nor welcome, sir. We'd gladly have either.
BALTHASAR. While we debate which is better, we'll part with neither.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. They're standing at the door, master. Tell them welcome.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. There's something in the air — we can't get in.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. You'd say so, master, if your clothes were thin. Your dinner's warm in there; you're standing here in the cold. It would make a man stark raving to be cheated like this.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Go, fetch me something — I'll break open the gate.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Break anything here, and I'll break your knave's skull.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. A man may break a word with you, sir, and words are but wind. Aye, and break it in your face, so long as he doesn't break it behind.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. It seems you want a breaking. Out upon you, peasant!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Here's too much "out upon you." Please, let me in.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Yes — when fowls have no feathers and fish have no fins.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Well, I'll break in. Go, borrow me a crowbar.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. A crow without feathers, master, is that what you mean? For a fish without a fin, here's a fowl without a feather. If a crow helps us in, sirrah, we'll pluck a crow together.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Go, get going. Fetch me an iron crowbar.

BALTHASAR. Be patient, sir. Oh, don't do it. In this you war against your own reputation, and bring under suspicion your wife's unblemished honour. Consider this: your long experience of her wisdom, her sober virtue, her years, and her modesty, all argue some cause on her side that you don't know about. Doubt not, sir — she will explain herself well as to why the doors are barred against you just now. Take my advice: leave in peace, let's all go to the Tiger for dinner, and toward evening, come yourself alone to learn the reason for this strange shut-out. If you force your way in now, in the busy traffic of the day, vulgar gossip will spring up about it. And that's exactly what the common mob will say against your hitherto-untouched reputation — gossip that will force its foul way in, and outlive you, lingering on your grave when you're dead. For slander breeds by succession, forever housed once it gets a foothold.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You've persuaded me. I'll leave in peace, and despite this lack of mirth, I mean to be merry. I know a wench of excellent conversation — pretty and witty, wild and yet gentle. We'll dine there. This woman I'm thinking of — my wife (but, I swear, without cause) has often thrown her in my face. To her we'll go for dinner. — You, go home and fetch the chain. By now I know it's made. Bring it, please, to the Porcupine — that's where the house is. That chain I'll bestow (if for no other reason than to spite my wife) on the lady there. Good sir, hurry. Since my own doors refuse to welcome me, I'll knock elsewhere, and see if they too disdain me.
ANGELO. I'll meet you there in an hour or so.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Do so. This joke will cost me some expense.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Luciana with Antipholus of Syracuse.]

LUCIANA. Can it really be that you've quite forgotten a husband's duty? Shall, Antipholus, even in the spring of love, your love's young shoots rot? Shall love, being built, become so quickly ruined? If you married my sister for her wealth, then for her wealth's sake treat her with more kindness. Or if you love elsewhere, do it in secret; muffle your false love with some pretence of blindness. Don't let my sister read it in your eye. Don't let your tongue be your own shame's spokesman. Look sweet, speak fair, dress up disloyalty. Clothe vice as the herald of virtue. Wear a fair face though your heart is corrupted. Teach sin to carry itself like a holy saint. Be secretly false. What need has she to know? What simple thief brags about his own guilt? It's a double wrong to play truant from your bed and let her read it in your face at the table. Shame, well managed, has only a bastard reputation; ill deeds are doubled by an evil word. Alas, poor women — at least make us believe, since we're made of trust, that you love us. Though others may hold the arm, show us the sleeve. We turn at your movement, and you can move us. So, gentle brother, go back in. Comfort my sister, cheer her, call her wife. It's a holy game to be a little vain when the sweet breath of flattery conquers strife.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Sweet mistress — whatever your name is besides, I don't know, nor by what wonder you hit upon mine — you show no less in your knowledge and your grace than the wonder of our earth, more than earthly, divine. Teach me, dear creature, how to think and speak. Lay open to my dull earthly understanding — smothered in errors, feeble, shallow, weak — the folded meaning of your tricky words. Why do you labour against my soul's pure truth to make it wander in an unknown field? Are you a god? Would you create me anew? Then transform me, and I'll yield to your power. But if I am still I, then I know well that your weeping sister is no wife of mine, and I owe no homage to her bed. Far more, far more, I incline to you. Oh, don't tempt me, sweet mermaid, with your song to drown me in your sister's flood of tears. Sing, siren, for yourself, and I'll be devoted. Spread your golden hair across the silver waves, and I'll take you as my bed, and lie there, and in that glorious fantasy I'll think a man wins by death who has such a way to die. Let love, being light, be drowned, if she sinks!
LUCIANA. What, are you mad, that you reason this way?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Not mad, but stunned — how, I don't know.
LUCIANA. It's a fault that springs from your eye.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. From gazing on your sunbeams, lovely sun, being near you.
LUCIANA. Gaze where you should, and that will clear your sight.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. As well shut my eyes, sweet love, as look on night.
LUCIANA. Why call me love? Call my sister that.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Your sister's sister.
LUCIANA. That's my sister.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. No. It is yourself — my own self's better part, my eye's clear eye, my dear heart's dearer heart, my food, my fortune, and my sweet hope's aim, my only heaven on earth and my claim to heaven.
LUCIANA. All this my sister is, or ought to be.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Call yourself sister, sweet — for it's you I aim for. You I will love, and with you I'll live my life. You have no husband yet, nor I a wife. Give me your hand.
LUCIANA. Oh, gentle, sir — hold still. I'll fetch my sister to gain her consent.
[Exit Luciana.]
[Enter Dromio of Syracuse.]
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why, what's this, Dromio? Where are you running so fast?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Do you know me, sir? Am I Dromio? Am I your man? Am I myself?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. You are Dromio, you are my man, you are yourself.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I'm an ass, I'm a woman's man, and beside myself.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What woman's man? And how beside yourself?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, besides myself, I'm promised to a woman — one that claims me, one that haunts me, one that will have me.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What claim does she lay to you?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, such a claim as you'd lay on your horse — she'd have me as a beast. Not because, being a beast, she'd have me — but because, being a very beastly creature, she lays claim to me.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What is she?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. A very respectable body — yes, such a one as a man can't mention without saying "begging your pardon" first. I have lean luck in the match, and yet she is a wondrously fat marriage.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What do you mean by a "fat marriage"?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, she's the kitchen wench, and all grease, and I don't know what use to put her to except to make a lamp out of her and run from her by her own light. I'll wager her rags and the tallow in them would burn a Polish winter. If she lives until doomsday, she'll burn a week longer than the whole world.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What complexion is she?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Dark like my shoe, but her face nowhere near so well kept. Why? Because she sweats — a man could go in over his shoes in the grime of it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. That's a fault water can mend.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, sir, it's ingrained. Noah's flood couldn't do it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What's her name?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Nell, sir. But her name plus three-quarters more — that's an ell and three-quarters — won't measure her from hip to hip.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. So she's broad, then?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No taller from head to foot than from hip to hip. She's spherical, like a globe. I could find countries in her.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where on her body is Ireland?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, sir, in her buttocks. I found it out by the bogs.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where Scotland?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I found it by the barrenness — hard, in the palm of her hand.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where France?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. On her forehead — armed and risen up, making war against her hair.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where England?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I looked for the white cliffs of chalk, but I couldn't find any whiteness on her. But I guess it stood on her chin, judging by the salty discharge running between France and it.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where Spain?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Honestly, I didn't see it — but I felt it hot in her breath.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where America, the Indies?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Oh, sir, on her nose, all over-decorated with rubies, carbuncles, sapphires, casting their rich light down toward the hot breath of Spain, who sent whole armadas of cargo ships to be ballasted at her nose.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Where stood Belgium, the Netherlands?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Oh, sir, I didn't look that low. To wrap up: this drudge or diviner laid claim to me, called me Dromio, swore I was promised to her, told me what private marks I had about me — the mark on my shoulder, the mole on my neck, the great wart on my left arm — that I, amazed, ran from her like she was a witch. And I think, if my chest hadn't been made of faith and my heart of steel, she would have transformed me into a stub-tailed dog and made me run in the kitchen wheel.

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Go, hurry, fly to the harbour. And if the wind blows any way from shore, I won't stay in this town tonight. If any ship sets out, come to the market, where I'll be walking until you return to me. If everyone knows us and we know no one, it's time, I think, to pack up and go.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. As a man would run from a bear to save his life, so I fly from her that would be my wife.
[Exit.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. There's none but witches living here, and so it's high time I was gone. The woman who calls me husband, my very soul abhors as a wife. But her lovely sister, possessed of such gentle sovereign grace, of such enchanting presence and speech, has almost made me a traitor to myself. But lest I become guilty of wronging myself, I'll stop my ears against the mermaid's song.
[Enter Angelo with the chain.]
ANGELO. Master Antipholus.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Yes, that's my name.
ANGELO. I know it well, sir. Look — here is the chain. I thought I'd find you at the Porcupine; the chain being unfinished kept me this long.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What do you wish me to do with this?
ANGELO. Whatever pleases you, sir. I made it for you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Made it for me, sir? I didn't order it.
ANGELO. Not once or twice, but twenty times you have. Go home with it and please your wife. Around supper time I'll visit you, and then collect my money for the chain.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Please, sir, take the money now — in case you never see chain or money again.
ANGELO. You're a merry man, sir. Farewell.
[Exit.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What to make of this I can't tell, but this I think: no man is so silly as to refuse such a fine offered chain. I see a man here needs not live by his wits, when in the streets he meets golden gifts like this. I'll go to the market and wait there for Dromio. If any ship puts out, then straight away.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Merchant, Angelo and an Officer.]

MERCHANT. You know the sum has been due since Pentecost, and since I haven't pressed you much, nor would I now, except that I'm bound for Persia and need money for my voyage — so settle up immediately, or I'll have this officer arrest you.

ANGELO. The very same sum I owe you is owed to me by Antipholus, and at the moment I met with you he received a chain from me. At five o'clock I'll collect the money for it. If you'll walk with me down to his house, I'll discharge my debt and thank you too.
[Enter Antipholus of Ephesus and Dromio of Ephesus from the Courtesan's.]
OFFICER. You can save yourself that trouble. Look — here he comes.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. While I go to the goldsmith's, you go and buy a rope's end. That I'll bestow on my wife and her accomplices for locking me out of my own doors in broad daylight. But quiet — I see the goldsmith. Off with you; buy a rope, and bring it home to me.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I buy a thousand pounds a year! I buy a rope!
[Exit Dromio.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. A man is well served who trusts to you. I promised your presence and the chain, but neither chain nor goldsmith arrived. Apparently you thought our friendship would last too long if it were chained together, and therefore didn't come.

ANGELO. Setting your joking aside — here's the bill, showing what your chain weighs to the last carat, the purity of the gold, and the costly workmanship, all of which comes to three ducats more than I owe this gentleman. Please, see him paid right away. He's bound for sea and only waits for that.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I don't have the money on me right now. Besides, I have business in the town. Good signior, take the stranger to my house, take the chain along with you, and tell my wife to pay the sum on delivery of it. Perhaps I'll be there as soon as you.
ANGELO. Then you'll bring the chain to her yourself?
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. No, you take it, in case I don't make it back in time.
ANGELO. Very well, sir, I will. Do you have the chain on you?
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. If I don't have it, sir, I hope you do — or else you can return without your money.
ANGELO. No, come on, please sir, give me the chain. Both wind and tide are waiting for this gentleman, and I, to blame, have already kept him here too long.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Good Lord, you use this dalliance as an excuse for your broken promise to come to the Porcupine. I should have scolded you for not bringing it, but like a shrew, you start the quarrel first.
MERCHANT. The hour is slipping away. Please, sir, hurry up.
ANGELO. You hear how he's pressing me. The chain!
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Well, give it to my wife and fetch your money.
ANGELO. Come, come, you know I gave it to you just now. Either send the chain, or send some token by me.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Enough — now you're running this joke into the ground. Come on, where's the chain? Please, let me see it.
MERCHANT. My business can't tolerate this delay. Good sir, tell me: will you answer me or not? If not, I'll leave him to the officer.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I answer you? What should I answer you?
ANGELO. The money you owe me for the chain.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I owe you nothing until I receive the chain.
ANGELO. You know I gave it to you half an hour ago.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You gave me none. You wrong me much to say so.
ANGELO. You wrong me more, sir, by denying it. Think about what this does to my reputation.
MERCHANT. Well, officer — arrest him on my suit.
OFFICER. I do, and I charge you in the Duke's name to obey me.
ANGELO. This affects my reputation. Either consent to pay this sum for me, or I'll have this officer arrest you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Consent to pay you what I never received? Arrest me, foolish man, if you dare.
ANGELO. Here's your fee — arrest him, officer. I wouldn't spare my own brother in this case, if he should scorn me so openly.
OFFICER. I arrest you, sir. You hear the charge.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I obey you until I can post bail. But sirrah, you'll pay for this fun as dearly as all the metal in your shop is worth.
ANGELO. Sir, sir, I'll have justice in Ephesus, to your notorious shame, I have no doubt.
[Enter Dromio of Syracuse from the bay.]

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, there's a ship from Epidamnum that's only waiting for her owner to come aboard, and then, sir, she sails. I've conveyed our cargo aboard, sir, and I've bought the oil, the balsam, and the brandy. The ship is in trim, the merry wind blows fair from land — they wait for nothing but their owner, master, and yourself.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. What's this? A madman? Why, you peevish sheep — what ship from Epidamnum is waiting for me?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. A ship you sent me to, to book passage.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You drunken slave, I sent you to buy a rope, and told you exactly what for and why.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. You sent me for a rope's end about as much. You sent me to the bay, sir, for a ship.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. I'll thrash this matter out at more leisure, and teach your ears to listen to me more carefully. Off to Adriana, villain, hurry. Give her this key, and tell her in the desk that's covered with Turkish tapestry there is a purse of ducats. Have her send it. Tell her I've been arrested in the street, and that will bail me out. Hurry, slave — go. On, officer, to prison until it arrives.
[Exeunt Merchant, Angelo, Officer and Antipholus of Ephesus.]

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. To Adriana — that's where we dined, where Dowsabel claimed me for her husband. She's too big, I hope, for me to embrace. There I must go, though against my will, since servants must do as their masters bid.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Adriana and Luciana.]

ADRIANA. Ah, Luciana — did he really try to seduce you like that? Could you tell, from a hard look in his eye, whether he was pleading in earnest or not? Did he look red or pale, sad or cheerful? What did you observe in this case from the meteors of his heart flashing across his face?
LUCIANA. First he denied that you had any claim on him.
ADRIANA. He means he gave me none — that's worse for me.
LUCIANA. Then he swore he was a stranger here.
ADRIANA. And true he swore, though by his vows he was a perjurer.
LUCIANA. Then I pleaded your case.
ADRIANA. And what did he say?
LUCIANA. The love I begged for you, he begged of me.
ADRIANA. With what arguments did he tempt your love?
LUCIANA. With words that, in an honest courtship, might move someone. First he praised my beauty, then my speech.
ADRIANA. Did you speak kindly to him?
LUCIANA. Have patience, please.

ADRIANA. I can't, and I won't hold my peace. My tongue, even if not my heart, will have its way. He is deformed, crooked, old, and withered — ugly-faced, worse-bodied, shapeless everywhere; vicious, rude, foolish, blunt, unkind; deformed in body, worse in mind.
LUCIANA. Who would be jealous of such a man? No evil's loss is mourned when it's gone.
ADRIANA. Ah, but I think him better than I say, and yet I wish others' eyes saw him worse than mine do. Far from her nest the lapwing cries away; my heart prays for him, though my tongue curses him.
[Enter Dromio of Syracuse.]
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Here, go — the desk, the purse, quickly, hurry!
LUCIANA. Why are you out of breath?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. From running fast.
ADRIANA. Where is your master, Dromio? Is he well?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, he's in a Tartar limbo, worse than hell. A devil in an everlasting coat has hold of him — one whose hard heart is buttoned up with steel; a fiend, a fairy, pitiless and rough; a wolf — no, worse — a fellow all in buff leather; a back-stabbing friend, a shoulder-tapper, one who blocks the passages of alleys, creeks, and narrow lanes; a hound that runs the wrong way and yet hunts well by scent; one who, before the judgement, carries poor souls to hell.
ADRIANA. Man, what's the matter?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I don't know the matter. He's arrested on the case.
ADRIANA. What, he's arrested? Tell me, on whose suit?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. I don't know on whose suit he's arrested, exactly; but he's in a suit of buff that arrested him — that much I can tell you. Mistress, will you send him his redemption — the money in his desk?
ADRIANA. Go fetch it, sister. This I wonder at —
[Exit Luciana.]
— that he should be in debt without my knowing. Tell me, was he arrested over a bond?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Not over a bond, but something stronger — a chain, a chain. Don't you hear it ring?
ADRIANA. What, the chain?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, no, the bell — it's time I was gone. It was two when I left him, and now the clock strikes one.
ADRIANA. The hours go backward! I never heard the like.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Oh yes — if any hour meets an officer, it turns back for sheer fear.
ADRIANA. As if time were in debt. How foolishly you reason!

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Time is a thorough bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth, season after season. Yes — and he's a thief too. Haven't you heard people say that time comes stealing on by night and day? If he's in debt and a thief, and an officer in the way, doesn't he have reason to turn back an hour in a day?
[Enter Luciana.]
ADRIANA. Go, Dromio. Here's the money — take it straight away, and bring your master home immediately. Come, sister, I'm weighed down with imagining; imagining, my comfort and my hurt.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Antipholus of Syracuse.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Every man I meet salutes me as if I were a well-known friend, and everyone calls me by my name. Some offer me money, some invite me places, some thank me for kindnesses, some try to sell me goods. Just now a tailor called me into his shop and showed me silks he'd bought for me, and went so far as to take my measurements. Surely these are just imaginary tricks — and Lapland sorcerers must live here.
[Enter Dromio of Syracuse.]
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, here's the gold you sent me for. What — have you got rid of the figure of old Adam in his new clothes?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What gold is this? What Adam do you mean?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Not the Adam who kept Paradise, but the Adam who keeps the prison — the one who walks in the calfskin that was killed for the Prodigal Son; the one who came behind you, sir, like an evil angel, and bid you give up your freedom.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I don't understand you.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No? Why, it's a plain case: the one who walked like a bass-viol in a leather case; the man, sir, who, when gentlemen are tired, gives them a sob and arrests them; the one, sir, who takes pity on decayed men and gives them suits of imprisonment; the one who plants himself to do more exploits with his mace than a soldier with a pike.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. What! You mean an officer?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Yes, sir — the sergeant of the company; the one who hauls anyone in to answer for breaking his bond; one who thinks a man is always going to bed, and says, "God give you good rest."
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Well, sir, you can rest there in your foolery. Is there any ship setting out tonight? Can we be gone?

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Why, sir, an hour ago I brought you word that the ship Expedition is putting out tonight, and then you were held up by the sergeant and made to wait for the slow boat Delay. Here are the gold angels you sent for to deliver you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. The fellow is out of his mind, and so am I, and here we wander in illusions. Some blessed power deliver us from here!
[Enter a Courtesan.]
COURTESAN. Well met, well met, Master Antipholus! I see, sir, you've found the goldsmith now. Is that the chain you promised me today?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Satan, get away! I charge you, don't tempt me.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, is this Mistress Satan?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. It's the devil.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. No, she's worse — she's the devil's mother. And here she comes in the costume of a light wench, which is why the wenches say "God damn me" — that's as much to say, "God make me a light wench." It is written that they appear to men like angels of light. Light is an effect of fire, and fire will burn; ergo, light wenches will burn. Don't go near her.
COURTESAN. You and your man are marvellously merry, sir. Will you come with me? We'll improve on our dinner here.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Master, if you do, expect baby food — or ask for a long spoon.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Why, Dromio?
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. By God, he must have a long spoon who must eat with the devil.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Get away, then, fiend! Why do you talk to me of supper? You're a sorceress — like all your kind. I conjure you to leave me and be gone.
COURTESAN. Give me back the ring of mine that you had at dinner, or, in exchange for my diamond, the chain you promised, and I'll be gone, sir, and not trouble you.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Some devils ask for nothing more than a fingernail clipping, a rush, a hair, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherry stone — but she, more greedy, wants a chain. Master, be wise; and if you give it to her, the devil will shake her chain and frighten us with it.
COURTESAN. Please, sir — my ring, or else the chain. I hope you don't mean to cheat me this way.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Begone, you witch! Come, Dromio, let's go.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. "Fly pride," says the peacock. Mistress, that you know.
[Exeunt Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse.]

COURTESAN. Now, no doubt about it, Antipholus is mad — otherwise he'd never behave like this. He has a ring of mine worth forty ducats, and in exchange for it he promised me a chain. Both he denies me now. The reason I conclude he's mad — besides this current display of rage — is a crazy story he told today at dinner, about his own doors being shut against him. Likely his wife, knowing his fits, deliberately shut the doors against him. My best move now is to hurry to his house and tell his wife that, being a lunatic, he burst into my house and forcibly took my ring. This is the wisest course, for forty ducats is too much to lose.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Antipholus of Ephesus with an Officer.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Don't worry about me, man, I won't run off. Before I leave you, I'll give you as much money as I'm arrested for, as a guarantee. My wife is in a contrary mood today, and won't readily believe the messenger that I should be under arrest in Ephesus. I tell you, it'll sound harsh in her ears.
[Enter Dromio of Ephesus with a rope's end.]
Here comes my man. I think he's bringing the money. How now, sir! Have you got what I sent you for?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Here's what, I promise you, will pay them all.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. But where's the money?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Why, sir, I spent the money on the rope.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Five hundred ducats, villain, for a rope?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I'll get you five hundred, sir, at that rate.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. To what end did I send you home?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. To a rope's end, sir; and to that end I've returned.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. And to that end, sir, I'll welcome you.
[Beating him.]
OFFICER. Good sir, be patient.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. No, it's me who needs to be patient. I'm the one in trouble.
OFFICER. All right now, hold your tongue.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. No, rather persuade him to hold his hands.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You whoreson, senseless villain!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I wish I were senseless, sir, so I wouldn't feel your blows.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You're sensible to nothing but blows — and so is an ass.

DROMIO OF EPHESUS. I am an ass, indeed; you can prove it by my long ears. I've served him from the hour of my birth to this very moment, and have got nothing from his hands for my service but blows. When I'm cold, he heats me with beating; when I'm warm, he cools me with beating. I'm woken with it when I sleep, raised with it when I sit, driven out of doors with it when I leave home, welcomed home with it when I come back. Yes, I carry it on my shoulders the way a beggar carries her brat; and I think when he's lamed me, I'll be begging with it from door to door.
[Enter Adriana, Luciana, Courtesan, and a Schoolmaster called Pinch.]
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Come, go along — my wife is coming over there.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Mistress, respice finem, respect your end — or rather, the prophecy like the parrot, "Beware the rope's end."
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Will you still talk?
[Beats him.]
COURTESAN. What do you say now? Isn't your husband mad?
ADRIANA. His rudeness confirms it. Good Doctor Pinch, you're a conjurer — restore him to his right mind, and I'll pay you whatever you ask.
LUCIANA. Alas, how fierce and sharp he looks!
COURTESAN. Notice how he trembles in his frenzy.
PINCH. Give me your hand, and let me feel your pulse.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. There's my hand — and let it feel your ear.
PINCH. I charge you, Satan, housed within this man, to yield possession to my holy prayers, and to your state of darkness fly straight back. I conjure you by all the saints in heaven.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Quiet, doting wizard, quiet — I am not mad.
ADRIANA. Oh, if only you weren't, poor distressed soul!

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You, minx — are these your customers? Did this fellow with the saffron-yellow face party and feast at my house today, while the guilty doors were shut on me, and I was refused entry to my own house?
ADRIANA. Oh, husband, God knows you dined at home. Would you had stayed there until now, free of these slanders and this public shame.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Dined at home? You villain, what do you say?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Sir, truth to tell, you did not dine at home.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Weren't my doors locked and me shut out?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. By God, your doors were locked, and you shut out.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. And didn't she herself abuse me there?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Without a doubt, she herself abused you there.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Didn't her kitchen-maid rail at, taunt, and scorn me?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Certainly she did — the kitchen-vestal scorned you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. And did I not depart from there in a rage?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. In truth, you did — my bones bear witness, having felt the force of his rage ever since.
ADRIANA. Is it wise to humour him in these contradictions?
PINCH. It's not a shame; the fellow finds his pattern, and by going along with him, he soothes his frenzy well.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You bribed the goldsmith to arrest me.
ADRIANA. Alas! I sent you money to free you by Dromio here, who came in haste for it.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Money, by me? Heart and goodwill, you might; but surely, master, not a scrap of money.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Didn't you go to her for a purse of ducats?
ADRIANA. He came to me, and I delivered it.
LUCIANA. And I'll witness with her that she did.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. God and the rope-maker bear me witness that I was sent for nothing but a rope.
PINCH. Mistress, both servant and master are possessed — I know it by their pale and deadly looks. They must be bound and shut up in some dark room.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Tell me, why did you lock me out today? And why do you deny sending the bag of gold?
ADRIANA. I did not, gentle husband, lock you out.
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. And gentle master, I received no gold; but I confess, sir, that we were locked out.
ADRIANA. You dissembling villain, you speak falsely about both.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. You dissembling whore, you're false in everything, and confederate with a damned crew to make a loathsome public mockery of me. But with these nails I'll claw out those false eyes that would behold this shameful sport with me as its target.
[Enter three or four people, who try to bind him. He struggles.]
ADRIANA. Oh, bind him, bind him! Don't let him come near me.
PINCH. More help — the fiend is strong within him.
LUCIANA. Oh me, poor man, how pale and wan he looks!
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. What, will you murder me? You, jailer, I'm your prisoner. Will you let them rescue me from you?
OFFICER. Masters, let him go. He's my prisoner, and you won't have him.
PINCH. Go, bind this man too — for he's frantic as well.
ADRIANA. What are you doing, you contrary officer? Do you enjoy watching a wretched man do violence and harm to himself?
OFFICER. He's my prisoner. If I let him go, the debt he owes will be required of me.

ADRIANA. I'll discharge that for you before I go from here. Take me right now to his creditor, and once I know how the debt arose, I'll pay it. Good Master Doctor, see him safely taken home to my house. Oh, most unhappy day!
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Oh, most unhappy whore!
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Master, here I'm taken into bondage for your sake.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Out on you, villain! Why are you driving me mad?
DROMIO OF EPHESUS. Would you be bound for nothing? Be mad, good master; cry, "the devil."
LUCIANA. God help, poor souls, how absurdly they talk!
ADRIANA. Take him from here. Sister, come with me.
[Exeunt Pinch and Assistants, with Antipholus of Ephesus and Dromio of Ephesus.]
Now tell me, on whose suit is he arrested?
OFFICER. One Angelo, a goldsmith. Do you know him?
ADRIANA. I know the man. What's the sum he owes?
OFFICER. Two hundred ducats.
ADRIANA. Tell me, how did it come due?
OFFICER. Due for a chain your husband received from him.
ADRIANA. He ordered a chain for me, but never gave it to me.
COURTESAN. When your husband, all in a rage, came to my house today and took my ring — the ring I saw on his finger just now — soon after I met him with a chain.
ADRIANA. It may be so, but I never saw it. Come, jailer, take me where the goldsmith is. I long to know the whole truth of this.
[Enter Antipholus of Syracuse with his rapier drawn, and Dromio of Syracuse.]
LUCIANA. God have mercy — they're loose again!
ADRIANA. And coming with naked swords! Let's call more help to have them bound again.
OFFICER. Away — they'll kill us!
[Exeunt, as fast as possible, frightened.]
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I see these witches are afraid of swords.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. The one who'd be your wife just now ran from you.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Come to the Centaur — fetch our things from there. I long for us to be safely aboard.

DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Honestly, stay here tonight, they'll surely do us no harm. You saw how they spoke politely to us and gave us gold. They seem to me such a kindly people that, except for the mountain of mad flesh claiming marriage with me, I could find it in my heart to stay here and turn witch.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I won't stay tonight for the whole town. So away — let's get our things aboard.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — The same
paragraphs: [Enter Merchant and Angelo.]
ANGELO. I'm sorry, sir, that I've held you up. But I swear he had the chain from me, though most dishonestly he denies it.
MERCHANT. How is the man regarded here in the city?
ANGELO. Of very respectable reputation, sir, infinite credit, much loved, second to none here in the city. His word could secure my whole wealth at any time.
MERCHANT. Speak quietly. Over there — I think — he's walking.
[Enter Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse.]

ANGELO. It's him; and that very chain about his neck which he so outrageously swore he never had. Good sir, come close, I'll speak to him. Signior Antipholus, I'm amazed that you would put me to this shame and trouble — and not without some scandal to yourself — denying with circumstance and oaths a chain you're now wearing so openly. Besides the cost, the shame, the imprisonment, you've done wrong to this honest friend of mine, who, if not for waiting on our dispute, would have hoisted sail and put to sea today. You had this chain from me — can you deny it?
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. I think I had it. I never denied it.
MERCHANT. Yes, you did, sir — and swore it on oath.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. Who heard me deny it or swear against it?
MERCHANT. These ears of mine, you know, did hear you. Shame on you, wretch. It's a pity you live to walk where any honest men gather.
ANTIPHOLUS OF SYRACUSE. You're a villain to accuse me like this. I'll prove my honour and my honesty against you immediately, if you dare stand and fight.
MERCHANT. I dare, and I do defy you as a villain.
[They draw.]
[Enter Adriana, Luciana, Courtesan, and others.]
ADRIANA. Stop, don't hurt him, for God's sake — he's mad. Some of you close in on him, take his sword away. Bind Dromio too, and take them to my house.
DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Run, master, run, for God's sake — take refuge. This is some priory. Inside, or we're done for.
[Exeunt Antipholus of Syracuse and Dromio of Syracuse to the priory.]
[Enter Lady Abbess.]
ABBESS. Be quiet, people. Why are you crowding in here?
ADRIANA. To fetch my poor distracted husband from here. Let us in, that we may bind him tight and carry him home for his recovery.
ANGELO. I knew he wasn't in his right mind.
MERCHANT. I'm sorry now that I drew on him.
ABBESS. How long has this possession held the man?
ADRIANA. This week he's been heavy, sour, and sad, much different from the man he was. But until this afternoon, his passion never broke into out-and-out rage.

ABBESS. Hasn't he lost much wealth through shipwreck? Buried some dear friend? Has not his eye wandered into unlawful love? A sin prevailing much among young men who give their eyes the liberty of gazing? Which of these sorrows is he subject to?
ADRIANA. To none of these, unless it's the last — namely, some love that often drew him from home.
ABBESS. You should have rebuked him for that.
ADRIANA. Why, so I did.
ABBESS. Yes, but not roughly enough.
ADRIANA. As roughly as my modesty would let me.
ABBESS. Perhaps in private.
ADRIANA. In company too.
ABBESS. Yes, but not enough.

ADRIANA. It was the substance of all our conversation. In bed he couldn't sleep for my pressing it; at the table he couldn't eat for my pressing it; alone, it was the topic of my speech; in company, I often referred to it; I kept telling him it was vile and bad.

ABBESS. And that's how the man went mad. The venomous clamour of a jealous woman poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth. It seems his sleep was disturbed by your scolding, and that's why his head is light. You say his food was sauced with your reproaches. Restless meals make poor digestion; from that, the raging fire of fever is bred — and what's a fever but a fit of madness? You say his pleasures were spoiled by your quarrels. With sweet recreation barred, what follows but moody and dull melancholy, kinsman to grim and comfortless despair, and at her heels a huge infectious crowd of pale ill-humours and enemies of life? To be disturbed in food, sport, and life-preserving rest would madden either man or beast. The conclusion, then, is that your jealous fits have driven your husband out of his wits.
LUCIANA. She never rebuked him but mildly, while he behaved roughly, rudely, and wildly. Why do you bear these reproaches and not answer?
ADRIANA. She has set me up to reproach myself. Good people, enter and seize him.
ABBESS. No, not a creature enters my house.
ADRIANA. Then let your servants bring my husband out.
ABBESS. Neither. He took this place for sanctuary, and it shall protect him from your hands until I have restored him to his senses, or wasted my effort trying.
ADRIANA. I will attend my husband, be his nurse, prescribe his diet through his sickness — for that's my role — and I'll have no proxy but myself. So let me have him home with me.

ABBESS. Be patient, for I won't let him stir until I've tried the proven methods I have, with wholesome syrups, drugs, and holy prayers, to make him a proper man again. It's part and parcel of my vow, a charitable duty of my order. So depart, and leave him here with me.
ADRIANA. I won't leave here without my husband. And it doesn't suit your holiness to separate husband and wife.
ABBESS. Be quiet and depart. You shall not have him.
[Exit Abbess.]
LUCIANA. Complain to the Duke about this indignity.
ADRIANA. Come, let's go. I'll fall prostrate at his feet, and never rise until my tears and prayers have won his Grace to come here in person and forcibly take my husband from the abbess.

MERCHANT. By now, I think the clock points to five. Soon, I'm sure, the Duke himself in person will come this way to the melancholy vale — the place of death and sorry execution behind the ditches of the abbey here.
ANGELO. For what reason?
MERCHANT. To see a respectable Syracusan merchant, who unluckily put in to this bay against the laws and statutes of this town, beheaded publicly for his offence.
ANGELO. Look, here they come. We'll witness his death.
LUCIANA. Kneel to the Duke before he passes the abbey.
[Enter the Duke, attended; Egeon, bareheaded; with the Headsman and other Officers.]
DUKE. Yet once again proclaim it publicly: if any friend will pay the sum for him, he shall not die — so much we care for him.
ADRIANA. Justice, most sacred Duke, against the abbess!
DUKE. She is a virtuous and respectable lady. It can't be that she has done you wrong.

ADRIANA. May it please your Grace — Antipholus, my husband, whom I made lord over me and all I had at your urgent letters, was today seized by a most outrageous fit of madness. He rushed desperately through the streets, his servant as mad as he, doing harm to the citizens by bursting into their houses, carrying off rings, jewels — anything his rage fancied. Once I had him bound and sent home while I went to settle for the wrongs he'd done here and there. Soon, I don't know by what strong escape, he broke from those guarding him, and he and his mad servant, each in raging passion, with drawn swords, met us again and, madly bent on us, chased us off — until, raising more help, we came back to bind them. Then they fled into this abbey, where we pursued them. And here the abbess shuts the gates against us, and will not let us fetch him out, nor send him forth that we may bear him away. Therefore, most gracious Duke, by your command, let him be brought forth and taken away for treatment.

DUKE. Long ago your husband served me in my wars, and I gave you a prince's word when you made him master of your bed, that I'd do him all the favour and good I could. Some of you, go knock at the abbey gate, and ask the lady abbess to come to me. I'll settle this before I move.
[Enter a Messenger.]

MESSENGER. O mistress, mistress, save yourself and flee! My master and his man are both broken loose, beaten the maids one after another, and bound the doctor, whose beard they've singed off with flaming brands, and as it blazed they kept throwing on him great pails of muddy water to quench the hair. My master preaches patience to him, while his man, with scissors, snips at him like a fool. And I'm sure (unless you send some immediate help) between them they will kill the conjurer.
ADRIANA. Quiet, fool — your master and his man are here. What you're telling us is false.
MESSENGER. Mistress, on my life, I tell you the truth. I've hardly drawn breath since I saw it. He's calling for you, and vowing, if he catches you, to scorch your face and disfigure you.
[Cry within.]
Listen, listen — I hear him, mistress! Run, be gone!
DUKE. Come, stand by me, fear nothing. Guard with halberds.
ADRIANA. Oh me, it's my husband. You see how he's carried about invisible. Just now we locked him in the abbey here, and now he's there — beyond all human reason.
[Enter Antipholus and Dromio of Ephesus.]

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Justice, most gracious Duke! Oh, grant me justice! Even for the service I once did you, when I rode beside you in the wars, and took deep wounds to save your life — even for the blood I lost for you then — now grant me justice.
EGEON. Unless the fear of death is making me delirious, I see my son Antipholus and Dromio.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Justice, sweet prince, against that woman there — she whom you gave me to be my wife, who has abused and dishonoured me to the very height of injury. Beyond imagination is the wrong she has shamelessly heaped on me today.
DUKE. Tell us how, and you'll find me just.
ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. Today, great Duke, she shut the doors against me while she feasted in my house with harlots.
DUKE. A grievous fault. Tell me, woman, did you do so?
ADRIANA. No, my good lord. Myself, he, and my sister dined together today. So befall my soul as this charge he lays on me is false.
LUCIANA. May I never look on day nor sleep at night if she's telling your Highness anything but the simple truth.
ANGELO. Oh perjured woman! They are both lying. In this the madman justly accuses them.

ANTIPHOLUS OF EPHESUS. My liege, I know what I'm saying. I'm not disturbed by wine, nor hot-headed, nor provoked by raging anger — though my wrongs might drive a wiser man mad. This woman locked me out today from dinner. That goldsmith there, if he weren't in league with her, could witness it, for he was with me then. He left me to go fetch a chain, promising to bring it to the Porcupine, where Balthasar and I were dining together. Our dinner over, and him not arriving, I went to look for him. In the street I met him, and in his company, that gentleman. There this perjured goldsmith swore I had received the chain from him today, which — God knows — I never saw. For which he had me arrested by an officer. I obeyed, and sent my servant home for certain ducats. He came back with none. Then politely I asked the officer to come with me to my house in person. On the way we met my wife, her sister, and a rabble of vile confederates. With them they brought one Pinch — a hungry, lean-faced villain, a mere skeleton, a quack, a threadbare juggler and a fortune-teller, a needy, hollow-eyed, sharp-looking wretch, a living corpse. This pernicious slave, no less, set himself up as a conjurer, and gazing into my eyes, feeling my pulse, and with no face at all, as it were, brazening it out against me, cried out that I was possessed. Then all together they fell on me, bound me, carried me off, and in a dark, dank cellar at home left me and my man, both tied together — until, gnawing my bonds in two with my teeth, I won my freedom and immediately ran here to your Grace, whom I beg to give me ample satisfaction for these deep shames and great indignities.
ANGELO. My lord, in truth, this much I will witness with him: that he didn't dine at home, but was locked out.
DUKE. But did he have such a chain from you, or not?
ANGELO. He did, my lord, and when he ran in here, these people saw the chain about his neck.

MERCHANT. Besides, I'll be sworn these ears of mine heard you confess you'd had the chain from him, after you first swore against it at the market. And on that I drew my sword on you — and then you fled into this abbey here, from which I think you've come by miracle.
